summary.name: Chaos Engineering (Netflix, IEEE Software article)
summary.one_liner: An article from Netflix engineers defining chaos engineering: experimenting on production distributed systems by injecting real-world failures to test steady-state availability.
keywords: how to test system failures in production
use_cases: Designing chaos engineering experiments for a distributed system
Testing whether services degrade gracefully when dependencies fail
Simulating regional outages to verify failover
Measuring the impact of failures on user-facing availability
Understanding Netflix's approach to production resilience testing
summary.what_it_does: The article explains chaos engineering as a discipline for building confidence in distributed systems by experimenting on them in production. It describes Netflix's Chaos Monkey (randomly terminating VM instances), Chaos Kong (simulating an entire Amazon region failing), and Failure Injection Testing (FIT) for making inter-service requests fail. It lays out four principles: hypothesize around steady-state behavior, vary real-world events, run experiments in production, and automate experiments to run continuously. It gives a method for experiments using a control group and an experimental group, with the stream-starts-per-second (SPS) metric as the key steady-state indicator.
notable: Netflix's Chaos Monkey, Chaos Kong, and FIT tools described as origins of the practice
Uses SPS (stream starts per second) as the primary steady-state health metric
Experiments compare control and experimental user groups rather than checking implementation against specification
caveats: Describes Netflix's internal in-house tooling; the article notes it is unclear how reusable the tooling is across organizations
Article is conceptual and reports that tooling and adoption questions remain open
Running experiments in production carries risk of harming the live system, as the article acknowledges
